message.content:
**Civil law**—the body of rules governing private rights and duties among individuals—is organized into several interrelated “components” or sub‑domains. While terminology can vary across jurisdictions, most modern civil‑law traditions share roughly the same core elements: | Component | What it Covers | Key Features | |-----------|-----------------|--------------| | **Sources of Law** | • Statutory codes (e.g., contracts, torts, property)
• Judicial decisions / precedents (in many civil‑law countries they serve more as guidance than binding authority)
• Customary practice & scholarly writings (doctrina) | Codified statutes dominate; judicial opinions often interpret but do not create new substantive law. | | **Substantive Law – Obligations** | Contracts, quasi‑contracts, delicts/torts, unjust enrichment, agency, partnership, corporate governance | Defines what parties owe each other, how those duties arise, and when they’re discharged. | | **Property Law** | Real estate ownership, possession, easements, mortgages, leasing, intellectual property | Governs acquisition, transfer, use, and protection of tangible/ intangible assets. | | **Family Law** | Marriage, divorce, child custody, alimony, adoption, surrogacy | Regulates personal relationships and parental responsibilities. | | **Succession/Wills** | Inheritance, wills, intestate succession, trusts | Determines distribution of estates after death. | | **Legal Procedure** | Courts’ jurisdiction, pleadings, discovery, trial process, appeals, arbitration | Provides mechanisms for enforcing rights and resolving disputes. | | **Evidence Rules** | Admissibility, burden of proof, witness testimony | Ensures fair presentation of facts before judgment. | | **Remedies & Enforcement** | Damages (compensatory, punitive, nominal), specific performance, injunctions, restitution | Specifies ways wronged parties may seek redress. | | **Jurisdictional Issues** | Personal vs. subject matter jurisdiction, venue, choice of law | Decides which court has power over a dispute and which laws apply. | ### How These Components Interact 1. **Statute → Substantive Rule** A statute might define *contract* formation requirements. When two parties enter a deal, their conduct is judged against this statutory framework. 2. **Contract + Tort Interaction** If one party breaches a contract, the injured party could also sue under tort theory if there was negligence involved. Both doctrines coexist within the obligation domain. 3. **Procedural Layer Over Substantives** Once a claim arises, procedural rules dictate filing deadlines, admissible documents, and evidentiary standards—all independent from the underlying substantive right being asserted. 4. **Remedy Selection** After determining liability via substantive law, the court chooses an appropriate remedy based on the nature of harm and policy considerations. 5. **Cross‑Domain Conflicts** For example, a real‑estate transaction involves both property law (title transfer) and contractual law (sale agreement). Disputes may touch multiple domains simultaneously. --- #### Quick Reference Checklist | Domain | Typical Legal Questions | |--------|-------------------------| | Contract | Did offer, acceptance, consideration exist? Are terms enforceable? | | Torts | Was duty owed? Did breach occur? Were damages caused? | | Property | Who holds title? Is encumbrance valid? | | Family | Does marriage meet legal criteria? Who gets custody? | | Succession | Whose will prevails? How are heirs determined? | | Procedure | Which court hears the case? What filings required? | | Evidence | Can this document be admitted? Who bears burden? | | Remedies | Should damages or specific performance be awarded? | Understanding these building blocks helps you navigate civil litigation, draft agreements, assess risks, and predict outcomes in everyday legal matters.
